entities.name: Cao Ang
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Cao Ang (177 CE – 197 CE) was the eldest son of the formidable warlord Cao Cao, a pivotal figure in the tumultuous late Eastern Han dynasty and the foundational period of the Three Kingdoms era in China. His brief but impactful life, centered geographically in the central plains of ancient China, is primarily remembered for his ultimate sacrifice at the Battle of Wancheng in 197 CE. This act of filial devotion and military courage directly enabled his father, Cao Cao, to escape a near-fatal ambush, an event that had profound ramifications for the subsequent political and military landscape of northern China and, by extension, the entire trajectory of the Three Kingdoms period. His death, while a personal tragedy for Cao Cao, became a critical turning point, preserving the life of the man who would eventually establish the Cao Wei state.

In 197 CE, Cao Ang accompanied his father on a campaign against Zhang Xiu, a minor warlord based in Wancheng (present-day Nanyang, Henan province). Initially, Zhang Xiu surrendered to Cao Cao, but a series of events, including Cao Cao's controversial relationship with Zhang Xiu's aunt, provoked Zhang Xiu to launch a sudden and devastating night attack on Cao Cao's camp. Caught off guard, Cao Cao's forces were thrown into disarray. During the chaotic retreat, Cao Cao's horse was killed, and he was gravely endangered. It was at this critical juncture that Cao Ang, along with his uncle Cao Anmin and the general Dian Wei, made a stand. Cao Ang selflessly offered his own horse to his father, ensuring Cao Cao's escape, while he himself remained to cover the retreat, ultimately perishing in the melee.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Cao Ang's sacrifice at Wancheng directly preserved the life of his father, Cao Cao, a figure whose survival was instrumental in the unification of northern China and the establishment of the Cao Wei state, fundamentally altering the trajectory of the Three Kingdoms period. His death was a critical turning point that allowed a major regional power to consolidate its control.
